title: Sourdough discard chocolate cake
subtitle: fudgy chocolate cake made with sourdough starter discard
excerpt: Sourdough starter discard adds a subtle tang and additional moisture to an otherwise standard chocolate cake batter. The result is a fudgier, more complex-tasting cake than one made without it, the fermented flour and water gives it the same gentle acidity that buttermilk provides in American chocolate cake. This is one of the most effective ways to use up discard that would otherwise be discarded.
sourceNotes: Using sourdough discard in non-bread baked goods became a widespread trend among home bakers from about 2015 onward, accelerated significantly during the 2020 home baking wave when many people maintained starters for the first time. The key insight, that unfed discard is in practice a fermented flour and water slurry with a mildly acidic pH, makes it useful wherever buttermilk or yoghurt would appear. Chocolate cake benefits particularly because the acidity of the discard reacts with the bicarbonate of soda in the recipe and deepens the colour and flavour of the cocoa.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze unfrosted layers well wrapped for up to 2 months.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Bake the day before. The cake is best on day 2 when the flavour has developed.

baking.bakeTemperatureNote: conventional 180°C or fan 160°C; skewer comes out with moist but not wet crumbs

content.text: Sourdough discard chocolate cake is fudgier and more flavourful than a standard chocolate cake. The discard brings mild acidity that reacts with the bicarbonate, deepening the colour and giving the crumb a slightly denser, moister texture. Use unfed discard at 100% hydration (equal weights flour and water); very old or heavily sour discard will make the acidity too pronounced.

Preheat the oven to 180°C conventional (160°C fan). Grease and line a 20 cm round tin. In a large bowl, whisk together the melted butter, eggs, vanilla extract, and sourdough discard until smooth. In a separate bowl, combine the flour, cocoa powder, caster sugar, bicarbonate of soda, and salt. Pour the wet ingredients into the dry and stir until just combined, don't overmix. The batter will be thick.

Pour the batter into the prepared tin and smooth the top. Bake for 35 to 40 minutes until a skewer inserted in the centre comes out with moist crumbs but no wet batter. The cake will be deeply coloured and pull away slightly from the tin sides. Cool in the tin for 15 minutes before turning out. Frost with chocolate ganache or a chocolate buttercream; the cake is also very good plain, lightly dusted with icing sugar.
